paper_title: Alloy: A Multi-Material Physics Engine for Robot Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU. We also report how throughput grows with the number of worlds, depth-camera throughput, agreement with closed-form references, and a reliability test over a thousand worlds.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Much of what useful robot must do involves things that are not rigid. kitchen robot pours and wipes. factory robot routes cables and seats connectors. laundry robot folds. Learning these skills in simulation needs two things at once. The first is physics for each material: cloth that drapes, liquid that flows, cables that bend. The second is scale: reinforcement learning tries task millions of times, so the simulation has to run in thousands of copies at once and stay correct in every one. Today these two needs pull apart. Engines built for robot learning at scale are at their best with rigid bodies. Solvers for cloth, liquids or granular material often come as separate programs with their own scene descriptions. team that wants robot arm to pour water often writes its own bridge between rigid-body engine and liquid solver, chooses time steps by hand, and builds its own checks for worlds that have quietly gone wrong. There is also new kind of user. More and more simulation code is written by coding agents, which read documentation, write scene, run it and read the errors. An engine that agents can use well needs short documentation that travels with the package, errors that say what to change, and way to tell broken simulation from bad policy. Alloy is our answer to these three problems. Its contributions are: One scene for many materials. Rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies are added through one Python interface. router assigns each object to solver suited to it and records why (Section 3.2). Correspondence: pranay@argonrobotics.ai. Code: https://github.com/argonrobotics-ai/alloy. Docs: https://alloy.argonrobotics.ai/docs/. 1 (a) Pouring water (b) Routing cable (c) Inserting cell into sprung holder (d) 1,024 parallel worlds of one task Figure 1: Scenes simulated in Alloy. (a) Franka arm pours water from bottle into glass; the water is simulated with Alloys liquid solver, coupled to the robots rigid-body contact. (b) Franka arm routes cable through clip toward socket; the cable is an articulated chain in the rigid-body solver. (c) gripper pushes an AA cell into sprung battery holder, simulated with rigid-body contact. (d) 1,024 parallel worlds of one robot task in single frame. Panels (a), (c) and (d) are rendered with Blender Cycles, (b) with Alloys path-traced camera. Coupling inside every control step. Solvers exchange poses and contact forces through proxy bodies, with step sizes chosen from the stiffness of the interface and refined per world when needed (Sections 3.3 and 3.4). health grade for every world. Each parallel world is graded OK, DEGRADED or INVALID; an invalid world is frozen while the others continue (Section 3.5). An interface made for coding agents. Documentation inside the package, errors that carry their fix, command-line tool that speaks JSON, and tool server for the Model Context Protocol (Section 3.7). Evidence from cold users. Agents that had never seen Alloy installed it and trained policies on single GPU; we report those results with their protocol, together with scaling, camera, accuracy and reliability measurements (Section 4). Alloy is open source under the Apache-2.0 licence and installs with pip install alloy-engine.

sections.title: 2 Background and Related Work
sections.content: Rigid-body engines for robot learning. MuJoCo [1] is the reference engine for articulated robots with contact. MuJoCo Warp [2] runs the MuJoCo model on GPU using Warp [3], framework that compiles Python functions into GPU kernels, and MuJoCo Playground [4] builds robot-learning environments on top of it. Orbit [5] (now Isaac Lab) and ManiSkill3 [6] provide large sets of GPU-parallel environments for manipulation and locomotion. Massively parallel simulation made it possible to train legged locomotion in minutes [7]. 2 Scene: objects, each shape and material card Router: one route per object, with reasons MuJoCo Warp rigid bodies, robots VBD cloth, soft bodies, rods Implicit MPM sand, pastes SPH liquids Coupler: proxy bodies exchange poses and contact forces; step sizes chosen per interface State, targets, Gym-style envs Health monitor: OK / DEGRADED / INVALID for every world Cameras: colour, depth, segmentation Figure 2: How scene becomes simulation. Each object is routed to one solver. When scene uses more than one solver, coupler joins them inside every control step. health monitor grades every parallel world after each exchange. Solvers for other materials. Vertex Block Descent (VBD) [8] simulates cloth and soft bodies by solving for one vertex at time and is stable with large steps. Smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) represents liquid as particles; its divergence-free variant [9] keeps the liquids volume constant. The material point method (MPM), brought to graphics for snow [10], handles granular material and pastes. Newton [11] gathers several such solvers in one GPU framework built on Warp, and Genesis [12] combines multiple solvers for robotics in one platform. Where Alloy sits. Alloy does not replace these solvers; it is built on them. Rigid bodies and robots step in MuJoCo Warp on GPU and in MuJoCo on CPU; cloth, soft bodies and elastic rods step in Newtons VBD; sand and pastes step in Newtons implicit MPM; liquids step in Alloys own SPH solver. What Alloy adds is the layer around them: one scene description, automatic routing, coupling with automatic step selection, health grading per world, cameras for every world, and an interface designed for agents. robot model written for MuJoCo (an MJCF file) loads in Alloy as it is.

sections.title: 3 System
sections.content: This section describes the engine as of version 0.1.2. Figure 2 gives the overview.

sections.title: 3.1 Scenes and cards
sections.content: A scene is list of objects. Each object is shape together with material card: small file that holds the materials measured values (density, stiffness, friction and so on) and their sources. The user never names solver. Listing 1 puts robot arm and tub of water in one scene; the arm is written in MuJoCos MJCF format.

sections.title: 3.2 Routing
sections.content: When the scene is built, the router gives every object one route. It decides from physical checks on the object, in fixed order. Static objects need no solver. Next comes phase: liquids, pastes and granular material are recognised from the card. Next comes shape class: rod, sheet or volume. Last comes rigidity: the router estimates how far the object would be squeezed under the grip force named on its card, compares that with the cards tolerance, and checks how 3 import alloy ARM = """<mujoco><compiler angle="radian"/><worldbody><body name="link1" pos="0 0 0.1"> <joint name="shoulder" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-2 2" damping="2"/> <geom type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.3 0 0" size="0.02" mass="1"/> </body></worldbody> <actuator><position joint="shoulder" kp="200" kv="10"/></actuator></mujoco>""" scene = alloy.Scene(dt=0.01) scene.add_ground() scene.add_robot("arm", mjcf=ARM, pos=(0, 0, 0.1)) scene.add_open_box("tub", inner=(0.08, 0.08, 0.05), wall=0.01, pos=(0.3, 0, 0)) scene.add_liquid("water", size=(0.064, 0.064, 0.024), pos=(0.3, 0, 0.024)) sim = alloy.build(scene, device="cpu") print({name: sim.routes()[name]["solver"] for name in ("arm", "water")}) sim.run(0.6, targets={"shoulder": (0.0, 0.3)}) print(len(sim.state(["water"], world=0)["water.points"]), sim.state(world=0)["arm/shoulder.q"].round(2)) print(sim.check()["ok"], sim.health()["worlds"][0]["severity"]) # {arm: mujoco, water: sph} # 1536 0.28 # True OK Listing 1: robot arm and water in one scene. The printed output shows the solver chosen for each object, the number of water particles and the joint angle, and the health of the world. much the whole body would bend. An object that passes is treated as rigid; one that fails is deformable. user can override the route for any object. Routes map to solvers as in Table 1. Every decision records the numbers it used and its margin to the nearest threshold, and sim.routes() returns the route, the solver and the reasons. user, or an agent, can therefore see why towel became cloth and why steel ruler did not. Solver Objects routed to it MuJoCo Warp (GPU), MuJoCo (CPU) VBD (Newton) Style3D (Newton) Film (Alloy, on VBD) Implicit MPM (Newton) SPH (Alloy) rigid bodies, robots, unclamped chains (such as cables), creased panels cloth, soft volumes, elastic rods anisotropic cloth when it is the only dynamic object paper, polymer film and metal sheets sand, pastes, viscous or yielding fluids liquids Table 1: Solvers and what the router sends to them.

sections.title: 3.3 Coupling
sections.content: If every dynamic object in scene uses the same solver, that solver steps alone and there is nothing to couple. When two or more solvers are present, they are joined in pairs, each with source and destination; by default the rigid-body solver is the source. The mechanism is proxy body, using Newtons proxy coupler with Alloys scheduler on top. The bodies of the source appear inside the destination as proxies that carry the sources poses and velocities. The destination solves its own contacts against these proxies. The contact forces it applied to them are then collected and fed back to the source. In this way towel pushes on robots gripper and the gripper pushes on the towel, while each solver keeps its own contact model. pair can also be one-way: the destination follows the source and no force is fed back. This is used for liquid whose mass is small beside the rigid bodies that drive it. 4 One such round is an exchange. Inside an exchange every solver steps once, in an order fixed by the graph of pairs. The default mode runs two passes. staggered mode repeats passes while some worlds interface residual, the disagreement between the two sides of pair, is above tolerance, up to cap. In the staggered mode the fed-back forces are relaxed per world with Aitkens method [13], which adapts the relaxation factor from one pass to the next. pair is strong when the destination adds more than half of the sources mass. Strong pairs into liquid run the staggered mode; other strong pairs, and most scenes with three or more solvers, use Newtons ADMM coupler [14]. Residuals are computed per world with order-independent operations, and world that has converged is frozen, so its result does not depend on which other worlds share the batch.

sections.title: 3.4 Choosing step sizes
sections.content: A control period of length (for example 10 ms) is split into 2j exchanges. The exchange interval = t/2j is the largest one that satisfies ωmax meff kc , (1) where meff is the effective mass at the interface between the two solvers, kc is the contact stiffness there, ωmax is stability constant (the largest allowed product of the interfaces natural frequency and the step), and < 1 is safety factor. Further caps apply, such as maximum exchange step. In words: stiff contact between light objects oscillates quickly and needs frequent exchanges; soft contact between heavy objects does not. Inside one exchange each solver then takes as many sub-steps as its own stability rule asks for; the liquid solver, for instance, uses its own limit on how far particle may move per step. The clock moves to finer step at once and returns to coarser one only after ten quiet periods. watchdog books the work done across every two-way interface. If that work is out of proportion to the worlds energy, or the two sides of an interface drift apart, the world escalates: it returns to the start of the control period and runs that period again with finer step. On first escalation only that world is run again, and every other world keeps its first result bit for bit; repeated escalations make the step finer for the whole scene.

sections.title: 3.5 A health grade for every world
sections.content: With thousands of worlds, some will meet conditions the solvers handle poorly, and learning algorithm will happily exploit broken world. After every exchange Alloys health monitor checks each world for non-finite values, penetration, excessive speed, jumps in energy, and exceeded joint or buffer limits. Each world is graded OK, DEGRADED or INVALID. An invalid world is returned to saved good state (by default the start of its control period) and frozen while the others continue. sim.check() returns one value to read after run, and sim.health() returns one row per world with the flags raised and, for each, the change that would fix it. Training code can use these grades to separate the physics failed from the policy failed.

sections.title: 3.6 Many worlds, cameras and robots
sections.content: A scene is replicated into many worlds that step together on one GPU; the same script runs on CPU. On GPU, chunks of up to 64 exchanges, with their sub-steps and coupler passes, are captured as graphs and replayed without returning to the host in between. In scene with robots, rigid bodies step at fixed 1.25 ms by default at 10 ms control period; scene of only free rigid bodies takes the largest stable step. Tight fits such as pegs, threads and connectors can be declared and receive extra contact handling. camera can be attached to every world and returns colour, depth and segmentation images. Environments follow the shape of Gymnasiums vector interface [15]: every world is one environment. 5 The package ships nine robots (two Franka arms, UR10e with two-finger gripper, two bimanual Franka setups, the Unitree G1 and H1-2 humanoids, the Unitree Go2 quadruped and the LEAP hand; most models come from MuJoCo Menagerie [16]), nine ready-made environments, legged-locomotion environments, 90 material cards and 118 object cards. further library of 5,423 object cards can be downloaded.

sections.title: 3.7 An interface for coding agents
sections.content: Alloy is written to be driven by an agent as well as by person. Documentation travels with the package. python -m alloy.docs prints the location of the guides, the runnable examples and an agent guide that were installed with the package, so an agent reads the documentation for exactly the version it is running. Errors carry their fix. Every error has message and fix field that says what to change; misspelt name lists the valid ones. command-line tool that speaks JSON. Every reply is one JSON object with either result or an error, its fix and the field at fault. tool server. alloy mcp serves the engine over the Model Context Protocol [17]: an agent can list the library, build scene, step it, read state, set targets, check health and render an image as tool calls. Helpers for building scenes. alloy.compose places library objects from sentence and checks the result with short simulation; alloy.create turns mesh, photo or description into checked object card.

sections.title: 4.1 Can a newcomer train with it?
sections.content: An engine for agents should be judged in the hands of an agent that has never seen it. We ran cold test. Eight independent sessions of coding agent (Claude Opus 5.5) each started on fresh virtual machine with one NVIDIA L4 GPU. Each installed Alloy from the Python package index and was allowed to read only what the package ships. Each wrote its own training and evaluation code. Success was computed from raw simulator state by the testers own script, on episodes whose random seeds differ from the training seed; we call these held-out episodes. Table 2 lists the results. All of them were measured on alloy-engine 0.1.0rc2, the pre-release that preceded the version described in Section 3, each from one training run. Intervals are Wilson 95 % intervals. Walking. The task is the shipped velocity-tracking environment for the Unitree Go2 on flat ground, trained with PPO [18] through the shipped trainer, which uses the rsl_rl library [7]. An episode succeeds if the robot does not fall and the world is not graded INVALID in 20 s, and its mean velocity stays within 0.25 m/s, and its turning rate within 0.25 rad/s, of the command over the last 15 s. Figure 3 shows held-out success against training time. The policy after 400 iterations was then pushed with 150 for 0.1 in random direction while walking at 0.5 m/s, harder push than any it met in training (at most 113 N). It was still standing at the end of the episode in 252 and 248 of 256 episodes on two seeds. 6 Task Training Training time Held-out success Walking: Unitree Go2, shipped environment, flat ground Push recovery: the same policy, pushed with 150 for 0.1 PPO, shipped trainer, 4,096 worlds 4.1 min 15.5 min 244/256, 95 % [92, 97] 497/512, 97 % [95, 98] as above 15.5 min 252/256 and 248/256, 9798 % Cable lift: task written by the tester PPO, shipped trainer, 1,024 worlds about 15 min about 30 min 242/256, 94.5 % [91, 97] 245/256, 95.7 % [93, 98] Pouring: shipped environment PPO, 512 worlds 38.5 min 118/128, 92 % [86, 96] Cup pouring: task written by the agent, on its second reward version Pick-and-place by imitation: shipped environment, gantry gripper, state observations PPO, 256 worlds about 70 min 256/256, 100 % [98.5, 100] behaviour cloning, 1,000 scripted demonstrations 66 256/256, 100 % [98.5, 100] Table 2: Policies trained by cold agents on one NVIDIA L4 with alloy-engine 0.1.0rc2; one training run per row; Wilson 95 % intervals in brackets. The two walking rows are the same run after 100 and 400 iterations, the second evaluated on two seeds; its times exclude the one-time compilation of GPU kernels. No evaluated episode in the walking or cable rows was graded INVALID. ) % ( c t - H 100 50 0 0 2 6 8 10 12 Training time (minutes) Figure 3: Go2 walking on one L4 with 4,096 worlds: held-out success against training time. Each point is 256 episodes on one evaluation seed. The one-time compilation of GPU kernels (202 on first use) is not counted. Cable lift. tester wrote this task: lift cable off table. An episode succeeds if every point of the cables centre line is above 3 cm at the last step. The shipped one-command trainer reached 94.5 % after about 15 minutes and 95.7 % after about 30. Pouring. In the shipped pouring environment an episode succeeds if at least 75 % of the water ends in the bowl. The checkpoint saved at 38.5 minutes of training succeeded in 118 of 128 held-out episodes. Another agent wrote its own cup-pouring task; on its second reward version, after about 70 minutes of training, the policy passed the same 75 % bar in 256 of 256 held-out episodes. Imitation. On the shipped pick-and-place environment with gantry gripper and state observations, tester collected 1,000 scripted demonstrations from 256 worlds and trained 7 three-layer network by behaviour cloning in 66 seconds. The object ended in the bin in 256 of 256 held-out episodes.

sections.title: 4.2 Throughput against the number of worlds
sections.content: Figure 4 shows how throughput grows when one scene is replicated into more worlds on one NVIDIA L4. Throughput is the number of simulated seconds produced per second of wall time, summed over the worlds. From 1 to 64 worlds it grows about 39 times for Franka Panda scene, about 20 times for cotton sheet on table and about 13 times for 200 ml pour; for three objects dropped in bin it grows about 377 times from 1 to 512 worlds. c l e n s a i 101 100 101 Three objects in bin Franka Panda scene 200 ml pour Cotton sheet on table 1 64 512 Parallel worlds Figure 4: Throughput against world count on one NVIDIA L4: physics only, 10 ms control period, one process, health check passed at every point. Rates are warm: control periods in which GPU graphs were first captured are replaced by the median of later periods. Four of the nine scenes of calibration set are shown, measured on development build before the first release; one run per point.

sections.content: Policies that learn from images need camera in every world. Table 3 gives the rate at which Alloy renders depth images for 1,024 worlds of Franka scene on one L4, with no physics between renders. second run on different L4 machine is shown beside the first. Adding segmentation to depth changed the cost by less than 1 %. sections.title: 4.4 Agreement with closed-form references
sections.content: Where physics has closed-form answer, simulator can be checked against it. Table 4 lists ten selected checks, each with the error Alloy measured against the reference and Alloys own tolerance for the check, set before it was run. They cover rigid-body motion and friction, the bending, twisting, sagging and buckling of rods, the pressure of liquid at rest and the stress of soft solid. 8 Check Reference Error Tolerance Pendulum period Momentum Sliding with friction Rope around post Rod bending under tip load Rod twisting Hanging cable Column under load Liquid at rest Soft solid under strain 8.0 106 small-angle period conservation of momentum 3.9 106 2.8 103 Coulomb friction law exact capstan equation 6.5 107 cantilever deflection 1.1 106 torsion formula 2.0 103 catenary sag 1.3 102 Euler buckling load 1.1 102 hydrostatic force on wall 2.8 103 neo-Hookean stress 1 103 1 103 1 102 2 102 1 102 1 102 1 102 5 102 3 102 5 102 Table 4: Ten selected closed-form checks: error against the reference and Alloys own tolerance, set in advance, both as defined by each check. All ten ran on CPU, on development build before the first release, one run each. Run at the time step set for that check rather than the default step.

sections.title: 4.5 Reliability over a thousand worlds
sections.content: A learning run uses every world, so rare failure matters. We stacked ten 5 cm blocks into tower in each of 1,024 worlds on one L4, with the starting positions shifted by up to 0.5 mm from world to world, and simulated 5 s. world counts as an error if any block moves or sinks by more than 1 cm or any value becomes non-finite. At each of Alloys three rigid-body settings (accurate, default and fast), and in two separate runs, 0 of 1,024 worlds had an error.

sections.title: 5 Scope
sections.content: Alloy is an early, 0.x release, and its interfaces may still change. What does not work yet is listed on one public page, each item with its measured size and what to do instead: https: //alloy.argonrobotics.ai/docs/keep-in-mind/.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Alloy lets robot-learning scene contain what real tasks contain: robots together with cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies. It chooses solver for each object, couples the solvers inside every control step with step sizes it derives itself, grades the health of every world, and presents all of this through an interface designed for coding agent working from the documentation that ships with the package. In cold test, agents installed pre-release and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on single GPU. Alloy is open source under Apache-2.0: pip install alloy-engine. Acknowledgements. Alloy builds on Newton, MuJoCo, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and ships robot models from MuJoCo Menagerie. We thank the authors and maintainers of these projects.
